Fatally Stabbed—Arrival of Prisoners.

Boise City, November 28th—A man by the name of George Kennedy, a packer, was stabbed this morning by a San Francisco hoodlum by the name of Jimmy Gates. Kennedy will die. The assailant was unprovoked, and Gates escaped, but was caught this afternoon about 4 o'clock at a China house near Boise river bridge, half a mile south of town. A large crowd gathered around him immediately and threatened to hang him. It was a hard work for the officers to escort him to the jail. There are still apprehensions that the mob will break the jail open and hang him.

I. B. Cowen, a Councilman from Shoshone county, arrived here this morning with three prisoners from Lewiston. Two are Indians, sent up for one and two years, for an assailant with intent to murder the Clerk at the Lapwai Ageney, and the other a Chinaman, sent up for robbery.

John Schilling brought to this office the other day a pair of deer horns sent by Dave Bunch, the boss hunter of Garden Valley. Their size, measuring 2 feet 8 inches between the two points furthest apart, will strike all old hunters as being something more than ordinary for those of the black tail or mule deer; but the strangest thing about the antlers is the arrangement of some of the points. From the first prong growing out of the main one, quite a number shoot off from all sides, forming a bunch of points at about the center of those of each antler, instead of all growing out from the same side, on nature's established plan. Within an inch or two
this we believe, though, is a common occurrence. Old hunters pronounce this a phenomenal pair of horns. They are now on exhibition in this office.

This is what the Dalles Times says about the town of Wallula: "This is fast becoming the "deserted village" of the Upper Columbia. The iron horse now snorts some distance away, and those who once received half-dollars from passengers stopping for meals and lodgings are now seeking other quarters. It is only visited now by the Snake River boats as a way station. The population has principally all moved to Texas Ferry, where they will try to make a livelihood at various avocations. It was never destined for a building site, and is the most forlorn looking place that man ever saw. The winds howl around the buildings, and the sand taken up by the hurricane can only be likened to a simoon.

A man named Cannady was stabbed in a saloon at Boise City at 4 o'clock Sunday morning by Gates, while they were playing at high-ball poker. There seemed to be nothing whatever to provoke the assault. Gates was standing looking over Cannady's shoulder when he reached around and stabbed him in the abdomen, inflicting a wound six inches deep. No one saw the knife in Gates' hand before the stabbing, and while in the act everybody that saw him thought he had reached down to pick up the balls. Gates was very low yesterday morning, and it was believed the wound would prove fatal. The affair created great excitement, and there was strong talk of lynching. Gates is under arrest.

samuel-l-perry.A2:
THE NEGRO FLIGHT.
THE NEGRO FLIGHT.

CONDITION OF THE FREEDMEN IN NORTH CAROLINA—HISTORY OF THE EMIGRATION MOVEMENT—POLITICAL RIGHTS SECURE AT HOME—FROM CERTAIN PLENTY TO PROBABLE WANT.

[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE HERALD.]

GOLDSBORO, Dec. 21, 1879.

This is conspicuously the exodus section. Within the past month between four hundred and five hundred negroes—men, women and children—have left the surrounding country for Indiana. At present there is a temporary lull in the exodus tide, attributable in part to unfavorable reports received from some who are now in Indiana, but mainly to lack of funds. The extent of the exodus feeling cannot be arrived at. It is difficult to place any estimate upon it, yet it is safe to say that in this Congressional district several thousands are ready to go regardless of consequences were their expenses to be paid. Some are now laying up their savings, awaiting further developments, while many appear unsettled in their intentions. Of those who have already left this State a few had sufficient means to take them to their destination, while the majority had barely enough to reach Washington, and some who had started were left behind for lack of money. Among the emigrants a few were reputed to be industrious and thrifty. One of them, with his boys, had cleared this year over $300 on his crop above all expenses. Others, less industrious, had lived from hand to mouth, as is characteristic of the negro.

BEGINNING OF THE MOVEMENT.

The Indiana scheme was begun here some months ago, and appears to have been inspired by one Langsdale, the editor of the Greencastle (Ind.) Banner, a republican newspaper. Langsdale had proclaimed that he would furnish homes to colored emigrants in Indiana, and his paper seems to have fallen into the hands of a notorious negro named Sam Perry, who taught a free school at Lagrange, about twelve miles from Goldsboro. Perry associated with him a negro preacher named Williams, and they soon succeeded in producing an exodus fever among the negroes, and it is said that by levying fees they made the excitement a source of handsome proft. Meetings were held in various sections and inflammatory speeches were made by Perry and others. Indiana was pictured as a perfect paradise for colored emigrants. They were promised plenty of work and wages—from $15 to $20 per month and board—good schools with the whites, and lands at from $1 to $3 an acre.

IMAGINARY WRONGS.

In connection with these promises and delusions the more ignorant of the race were made to believe that all sorts of imaginary wrongs were being practised upon them here. It was told them, for instance, that they could not here get credit at the stores, while in Indiana it would be readily accorded them. Their worst fears, passions and prejudices were worked upon. They were told by some that if they renamed here, should the democrats elect the next President they would be thrust back into slavery and other similar nonsense. The negro is of a decided migratory disposition, and while many of those who have gone barely knew whether Indiana was a State, a county or a city, yet the very idea of a grand excursion infatuated them so that they disposed of their little effects for a mere trifle and recklessly started out on their journey.

Agents are still among the negroes here urging others to go, and another party is advertised to leave in a few days, but the movement will hardly reach any considerable extent until further tidings are received and more money is furnished. The return of one of their representatives now in Indiana is anxiously awaited here. Should he bring a favorable report—and it is feared that designing men will induce him to make such a one—the exodus will doubtless receive a strong impetus. He is expected soon.

A CAUSELESS MOVEMENT.

As for the cause of the exodus, there is none. The white people here generally regret it and deprecate the departure of the negroes from North Carolina. The farmers in particular are laboring under considerable uncertainty as to their future crop arrangements. The more intelligent of the colored race, too, are openly opposed to the scheme; but, strange as it seems, neither their political white leaders nor the intelligent of their own color can induce them to halt. They feed on castles in the air—day dreams of fame and fortune. All admit that they are being treated well in North Carolina and that their condition has very much improved within a few years. Large numbers own houses and lots, and not a few own valuable farms. The white people generally are pleased at the thrift of the colored people. The industrious negroes find no trouble in leasing good lands for farming purposes, and on the most favorable terms.

This class of people are very much sought after by
the thrift of the colored people. The industrious negroes find no trouble in leasing good lands for farming purposes, and on the most favorable terms. This class of people are very much sought after by landowners, and are gladly supplied by the landlord with teams, implements and provisions at most reasonable prices, to be paid for out of the crops in yearly instalments. Those who are industrious and economical generally find their labors rewarded and themselves in the possession of a handsome surplus after paying for advances and rents, while others, who neglect their crops and lack capacity to manage for themselves, may not do so well.

POLITICAL CONDITION.

The negroes are perfectly secure in their civil rights, and, while some of the whites may have prejudices, the more intelligent masses form a strong conservative element, and the negro is sure of protection. The State has provided the same educational facilities for the colored as for the white children, the races being separately educated. The colored schools generally are well patronized, even by adults, and the children make rapid progress. The colored free school here is in a most flourishing condition and is kept up eight months in each year. It is taught by three competent teachers. The democratic Legislature of this State has established a normal school at Fayetteville, where colored teachers for free schools are being educated at the expense of the State. It also appropriated $50,000 for the construction of an asylum for the colored insane, and another appropriation will probably be made for this institution by the next Legislature. The building is being erected near this town and is a very handsome edifice. It will be completed by next March, with accommodations for 125 patients. There is also an institution at Raleigh for the colored deaf, dumb and blind maintained by the State. There are about twelve well equipped colored military companies in the State. They form part of the State guards, and have been formed under the present democratic administration. The company at this place is named the Vance Guards, after Senator Vance.

NEGRO INDUSTRY AND SKILL.

The industrial State fair of the colored people, held at Raleigh last month, was in every way creditable to their race. It was planned and conducted by them, though most of the premiums were donated by whites. The fair was opened by Governor Jarvis, wnid, with other gentlemen, was escorted to the grounds by the colored military. Politically, the rights of the negroes are fully protected. They can vote in every election. Our courts of justice are as open to them as to the whites. Colored men serve on juries, and this, too, in trials altogether confined to whites. samuel-l-perry.A5:
A SEQUEL TO THE EXODUS.
How North Carolina Democrats are Trying to Get Even.
How North Carolina Democrats are Trying to Get Even.

A requisition from the governor of North Carolina for Samuel L. Perry, wanted in that state on the charge of forgery, arrived here yesterday in the hands of Sheriff George K. Bigby. Chief-Justice Cartter issued a warrant. The man was arrested by Bailiff Dorsey and brought before his honor, sitting in chambers, at 2 o'clock. Hon. Jere Wilson and Professor R. T. Greener appeared for the accused and R. S. Davis, esq., for the state of North Carolina. The indictment accompanying the requisition charges that Samuel L. Perry on December 20, 1878, forged an order, in the name of the school committee, on the treasurer of Lenoir county, directing him to pay out of the public-school money, to the credit of school district No. 15 for the colored race, $45 for pay of Aaron E. Perry as teacher. Mr. Wilson stated that he was not ready to proceed with the hearing, having just come into the case, and to allow him time to prepare an adjournment was taken until to-morrow noon.

When the circumstances connected with this action of the North Carolina authorities is investigated a little, as has been done, it looks very much like a case of political persecution. Perry in the first place denies that he ever committed the forgery and has repeatedly asked for a trial within the past few years, but failed to obtain one. He, shortly after the indictment was found, was placed under $100 bonds to appear, and was then told that he would be notified when wanted. Such notification has never reached him. In 1878 and the early part of 1879 he lived in North Carolina undisturbed, because he did nothing to excite the ire of the "tar heelers." But in the summer of 1879 he was less fortunate. Seeing the degradation and actual slavery to which his people were subjected, he determined to assist in their amelioration if it could be accomplished. He, together with P. C. Williams, began and carried into effect the exodus movement. They banded together large numbers of their race, and, with the assistance of outside help, much of which came to this city, had them transported to the state of Indiana. Perry and Williams made repeated visits to the hoosier state to see their people located and secure them employment. In this respect they were remarkably successful. All this time Perry was traveling to and from North Carolina, agitating the exodus and assisting to release his colored brethern from bondage. The indictment meanwhile lay among the court files, but not a word was said about bringing him to trial on the charge, and until recently it was supposed that the case would never be heard of again. Recently there was an election in the state of Indiana, and the news has just reached North Carolina; also the fact that all the colored people emigrating there a year or more ago voted, and cast their ballots in favor of the republican candidates. When the "tar-heelers" heard this, and realized the fact that Perry was the main-spring of that movement, it is evident they determined to "get even" with him for the part that he had taken in bringing about a democratic defeat in Indiana. The old indictment was hunted up, a requisition obtained and the sheriff sent here to get his man. Perry said yesterday that he had no fears as to the result of a trial if accorded a fair one, but his case would never reach a hearing. If they once got him into the state of North Carolina his life would not be worth much to him, and they would not hesitate to kill him at the first opportunity. That is his reason, and the only one, for not wishing to go at this time.

Perry was later in the day released on bonds, Major A. C. Richards appearing as his surety.

The Alleged Exodus Leader, Perry.
PROCEEDINGS IN COURT TO-DAY.
The Alleged Exodus Leader, Perry.
PROCEEDINGS IN COURT TO DAY.
This morning, in the room of the Court, in
L. Perry, the colored man alleged to have led the North Carolina exodus, who was arrested on a bench warrant on Monday last, based on a requisition from North Carolina, where he is indicted for forgery, was resumed—Messrs. Shellabarger & Wilson and R. T. Greener for the prisoner, and Messrs. R. T. Merrick and R. S. Davis for the state of North Carolina.

Mr. Shellabarger said that probably he should address the Court as "Your Excellency," and he had concluded to call the attention of the Court to a few points. He called attention to the case of Kingsbury (106 Mass, 223), as an authority that the papers may be examined. They would rely on the doctrine in the Dennison case (24th Howard), which he claimed means that the indictment is an artificial structure, and which as an entirety is required to have certain fixed elements. It may be defective as an indictment, and yet be good as a statement of a crime. The executive should inquire if a crime had been committed.

The court said that he coincided with Mr. Shellabarger's views. He had made up his mind to see if a crime had been committed. After he made investigation and found that an attempt had been made to establish a crime, could he go further and see if the paper was sufficient to warrant the prisoner's rendition. He had made up his mind to see if a crime had been committed; whether the prisoner was a refugee or fugitive from justice, and whether the application was in good faith. He did not believe that it was contemplated that the executive should be made the instrument of rendition for an in direct or sinister purpose. How far he could go in investigating the case was the question with him.

Mr. Shellabarger expressed his gratification that the court had come to the conclusions he had expressed, and he claimed that the charges in the indictment must be clearly and implicitly set forth, otherwise it was faulty. He proceeded to read authorities in 56th New York and other volumes.

POLITICS IN THE CASE.

He closed by remarking that they are acting on information which led them to believe that the object of this proceeding was quite inferior to the objects which appear in the papers, and if this man is extradited it may result in disaster.

Mr. Merrick said he was at a loss to understand the ominous remark. As far as he was concerned he knew nothing of any other purpose than that which appears on the papers. He was willing now that the doors be thrown upon, and if they could show this he would say let the man go.

Mr. Davis said that the agent of the state, Mr. Bagley, had never served a writ in his life, but in the interest of the colored people he volunteered to come here with the requisition.

Mr. Shellabarger said that his remark was not intended to reflect on counsel, but that they (counsel for defendant) were acting on the belief that there was an object outside of the papers. They had information that if this man was taken back to North Carolina the chances are that he will be destroyed.

Mr. Merrick.—That is a more extraordinary statement than the proceeding one.

The Chief Justice.—Go on with your case.

Mr. Greener at 11:05 o'clock commenced his argument, saying the drift of the decisions was that the executive could examine as to the crime and the object, and claimed that in the Kimpton case in 1878 the doctrine was plain. He would admit that there may be any form of indictment. Fortunately the officer here sat both as a judge and an executive, and he proceeded to claim that it must be shown that a crime had been committed. They were able to show that on account of certain political services and certain disturbances they desired to get the prisoner to North Carolina.

Mr. Davis said that he could not see why this stuff should be interjected in the case. He denied that this man would have any other than a fair trial, for there had not been a jury on which from 3 to 10 negroes had served for 10 years and 6 or 8 were on the grand jury who found this bill. He hoped this political stuff would be kept out.

Mr. Greener answered that had Mr. Davis had the same experience he (the speaker) had in North and South Carolina he would probably not be sure that a negro would have a fair trial there. He was glad that the other side had admitted that this Mr. Bagtey, the agent, was not a legal officer and he was not sure but that they knew him. He could not say that he was the same man, but his name and initials are the same as one Mr. Bagbey, who some few years ago took out nine negroes and cutting their throats threw their bodies into the Neuse river. It may be that they could show that he was the same party. The prisoner recognized him as the man, and hence his fear of being returned to North Carolina in his charge. Mr. Greener said that the prisoner never was a fugitive from justice, and when he was indicted friends came up and went his bail. He was here temporarily only, and would have gone back to North Carolina long since for trial, had he been called on with the assurance that he would have had a fair trial. After reading several other authorities, Mr. Greener said the chief justice should take into consideration the lapse of time and the small amount involved, and they would show that there were political motives in this proce ding. The chief justice had the power to exercise executive discretion. The object of the proceeding, he said, was transparent, and there was no doubt of the policy, expediency and justice of exercising discretion in favor of the prisoner and declining to remand him. If afterwards it was found to be wrong, the only party injured would be the state of North Carolina, to the extent of $45. In this case it was within the province of the Chief Justice to stand between a man and disaster, and vindicate the principles of the constitution, giving to a man the right of a fair and impartial trial and the boon of liberty.

Mr. Davis disclaimed any ulterior motive actuating him, and if he thought for a moment that there was any other object sought in what appears by the papers he would abandon the case at once. There was no man living who would do more than he in defending the rights of the colored man.

The Chief Justice said that he believed that it was his duty to examine as to the objects sought by the process—whether there was any other service than that contemplated by the constitution sought. He directed the attention of the counsel to the question of authentication.

Mr. Merrick at noon commenced his argument, and referring to the statement of Judge Shellabarger that there was an end sought not apparent on the face of the papers, he said why have they not brought forward some proof. He did not know that they intended that this statement would have its weight with the court. While they knew that he (Judge C.) and the counsel for the prisoner were in political sympathy he thought they did him wrong if they supposed that such statement would affect his judgment. This question is as was that in most of the cases quoted in relation
pathy he thought they did him wrong if they supposed that such statement would affect his judgment. This question is as was that in most of the cases quoted in relation to a colored man or as Mr. Greener says 'a negro.' Special Correspondence of the Alexa Gazette. Washington, D.C. WASHINGTON. D.C. OCT. 28, 1880.
The republicans here, from some cause or other, have hauled in their horns amziogly during the last few days, and are now singing slow music. Whether it is a faint or not is of course unknown to any bus themselves, but that it is so all are aware who talk to them.

United States Senator Hereford, of West Virginia, is here to day. He says the democrats of that State will send a solid congressional delegation to Congress. Another gentleman from that State says the contest for United States Senator there is between Mr. Hereford and Mr. Camden, with chances greatly in favor of the former.

The negro men in Washington are rapidly thinning out, and though usually there are more of them than of white men on the streets, the sight of one is now quite a rarity. Of course they have all been sent away to cost fraudulent votes for the radicals, some, it is said, to Alex andrie.

Notwithstanding the denials of the British officers in Canada, the War Department is disposed to credit the evidence of the scout Aliison about the desire of Sitting Bull to surrender to the United States, and should it be so will entrust the whole negotiation to Gen. Terry, as he is on the ground, is familiar with the matter and as the government has full reliance in his judgment.

From some unexplained cause there has been an entire revulsion in the feelings of the democrats here during the last day or two, and from being in the slough of despond they are to day as cheerful as though the Indiana election had never occurred, and talk confidently of Hancock's else ion, and that, too, by a vote large enough to deter the radicals from their contemplated and already arranged plan of seizing the government in case of a close vote, as they did four years ago. They say that the fusion ticket in Maine is bound to succeed; that the greenback vote of Indiana (15,000) has been secured for Hancock, which will give him the State by 8,000 majority; that California and Nevada are safe, and that New York is as sure for him as Texas. With regard to Virginia they think all danger is now removed, as the proof that the Mabonites' real purpose is to defeat Hancock has become so apparent that it will be impossible for any man who pretends to be a democrat to vote their ticket. Intelligence from Virginia received here to day is to the effect that the democrats are making a determined effort to bring out a large vote, and that the probability is that the vote for the regular democratic ticket will be as large as was given Mr. Tilden in 1879. Both parties in the State are paying the capitation tax of their delinquents to the extent of their ability, but the negroes are a long way in the rear, and their vote will be considerably smaller than it was four years ago.

Detailed accounts of the defeat of Victoria's band of Indians by the Mexicans were received at the War Department to day. They represent that the Chief fought gallantly, and was killed on the battle field. The Mexicans took a number of prisoners, among them some women and children, the disposal of whom will become an international question, as neither this country nor Mexico wants them.

Quite a large number of the residents of this city, including delegations from some of the secret societies, attended the funeral of the late Hugh Latham, esq., in Alexandria, to day. The remainder of Mr. Latham's term as mail contrsor for the U. S. House of Representatives will be filled by his son, R. M. Latham.

The arrest of one of the editors of the New York Truth, which first published Garfield's Chinese letter, upon the charge of libel and not forgery, is commented upon here very freely today as indicating that with all their denials of the authorship of that letter they are not so sure that he did not write it after all.

The government is doing its best to shield Perry, the exodus negro forger, and to prevent him from being taken to North Carolina where his crime was committed, and will doubtless succeed. When the government prostitutes its powers to the protection of criminals, its honest subject are in a bad way.
samuel-l-perry.A18:
THE PERRY CASE.
The Requisition Honored and Habeas Corpus Proceedings Commenced.
The chamber of the supreme court of this District was packed with people yesterday morning to witness the proceedings before Chief-Justice Cartter in the case of Samuel L. Perry, wanted on the requisition from the governor of North Carolina to answer the charge of forgery in that state.

The counsel on both sides were all in attendance. His honor inquired if either side had anything further to advance in regard to the case.

Mr. Wilson said that they had deemed it prudent if the conclusion reached by his honor should be against them to petition for a writ of habeas corpus in order that the case might be passed upon judicially.

Mr. Merrick responded that their side had no disposition to prevent it, but would permit every opportunity to expedite it.

Chief-Justice Cartter then proceeded to deliver a lengthy opinion, covering the points presented in the case, and at the close directed that Perry be delivered into the custody of the agent of North Carolina.

Mr. Wilson immediately called him to the clerk's desk, and he swore to a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, setting forth that he was unlawfully detained in the custody of George K. Bagbey, on an order of Chief-Justice Cartter, he having been arrested by virtue of a requisition from one Thomas J. Jarvis; that said requisition is insufficient and illegal; that the alleged crime is not properly certified to; that he is not guilty of said alleged offense; that he has not fled the jurisdiction; and, further, he believes that his extradition is not sought in good faith, but because of his relation to certain political affairs, including the so-called negro exodus, and that he believes that if he is sent to North Carolina he will be in great bodily danger.

The writ was issued by Justice Wylie and made returnable before him forthwith, which was done by Sheriff Bagbey. The hearing was set down for November 5 and Perry was released on $1,000 bail, Major A. C. Richards becoming his security.
samuel-l-perry.A25:
The Alleged Exodus Leader.
HEARING ON HABEAS CORPUS.
The Alleged Exodus Leader.
HEARING ON HABEAS CORPUS.

This morning, Samuel L. Perry, colored, who has the reputation of having led the negro exodus from North Carolina to Indiana, was before Judge Wylie, sitting at chambers in the Columbia Law Building. It will be remembered that last Monday week Mr. George K. Bagbey, the agent of the state of North Carolina, presented to Chief Justice Cartter a requisition from Gov. Bayley for Perry, he being charged in an indictment of the supreme court of Lenoir county, North Carolina, with forgery. He was arrested and subsequently the case was argued by Messrs. Shellabarger & Wilson and R. T. Greener for Perry and Messrs. R. T. Merrick and R. S. Davis for the state. Chief Justice Cartter decided to surrender the prisoner, and made an order placing Perry in the hands of Mr. Bagbey. A petition was at once presented to Judge Wylie for a writ of habeas corpus, and the writ was ordered to issue, and the case under the writ was, under the stipulation of counsel, set by Judge Wylie for hearing this morning. When the case was called this morning an additional return was made by Mr. Bagbey to the effect that Perry had stated that he had forfeited the bond and could not be taken back and admitted that he had fled from the state to evade trial. Mr. Bagbey denies that the proceedings were taken on account of any political reasons, or that it was because Perry had been connected with the so-called "exodus movement," and states further that he would take Perry and deliver him to the authorities of Lincoln county, and would permit no one to molest him, and should he be surrendered he has no doubt but that he will have a fair trial. Mr. Bagbey makes this return in the form of an affidavit, and accompanies it by another from W. W. S. O'B. Robinson, a candidate on the republican electoral ticket, that he was the counsel for Perry in the prIMARY hearing, and he can see no reason why Perry, if brought back, cannot have a fair and impartial trial.

After some discussion as to the mode of procedure, Judge Wylie decided that the case must go on.

Mr. Wilson said he had prepared a demurrer to the return that it was insufficient because there was no valid indictment in the case or lawful authentication thereof. He also read an affidavit of Perry denying the allegations in the return, and specifically those as to his ad-
there was no vand indictment in the case of lawful authentication thereof. He also read an affidavit of Perry denying the allegations in the return, and specifically those as to his admissions. He also avers that it is impossible for him to have a fair trial there, and that the proceedings are for the purpose of getting him to the state and punishing him for political purposes.

TESTIMONY OF PERRY.

Samuel L. Perry, the petitioner, under objection by the state, testified that from 1867 to 1879 he lived in Lenoir county, North Carolina; was raised and resided in Chatham county prior to 1867; taught school from 71 to 78; had a first grade certificate drawing the highest pay—$40 per month. He owned a town lot in the town of Lagrange, which he valued at $1,000 or $1,200; there was a dwelling house and office on the lot. Had been connected with the political affairs of the state, always taking an active part, from 19 years of age; was president of several union leagues, and saw that the voters were all registered, keeping them up till they had voted; had defeated all the prominent republicans in the county for delegate to the congressional convention. After the defeat in 1876 they kept waiting for things to get better, and he turned his connection to something else, but was active again in 1878. Witness was connected with the exodus; having subscribed to the New York Herald, he saw notices of the exodus from Mississippi, and the people were stirred up to go to Kansas; he made several speeches, advocating the movement, in the neighboring counties, having agents in others. The first organization was in April, 1879, but it was secret on account of the white people getting mad about it, and some of his best white friends did not speak to him. There was one society of 1,500, including women. It was pretty well known that he was the head of the movement. Some of the papers—the Goldsboro Messenger—advocated putting him out of the way. They concluded to get away, and Bishop Hood's paper advised those who intended to emigrate to send an agent first; they then met and L. C. Williams and himself were sent out to look for a suitable place, and they left on September 15th, 1879, having 150 persons, who were to constitute a colony to settle where they selected a place. They left because they could not get along and could not get justice at the inferior court, composed of magistrates, the most bitter democrats in the state. They arrived here and remained 13 days. While here he was interviewed by Mr. Dupray, of the N. Y. Times, and Mr. Godwin, of the Republican. The Times published the interview September 23d, 1879. Quite a number of papers were sent to North Carolina and some of the democratic papers published portions of these articles. Went from here to Indianapolis and remained there 8 or 10 days and then to Greencastle. Witness and Williams then went back (stopping in Baltimore and this city) to Lagrange, N. C. Witness while in Baltimore wrote what day they would be there and he received letters warning him not to come. He, however, went and got off the train before reaching the depot. He remained about twenty days, but not at his own home, because he was advised it would be dangerous. Remained from home because he believed that he would be murdered. He was not out of the presence of at least 20 men while he was there and they were armed for his protection. Witness attempted to sell his property and put it in the hands of the postmaster for sale for what he could get for it. Witness after he said he could not sell it put out some advertisements. Sold it for $61 in money and $14 in trade. When he came away there were about 150 men accommodated him; never staid two nights in the same house; the places where he stopped were kept secret. Had not been back to Lagrange since. He was a witness before what was known as the Exodus committee; had received a letter from Jerry Williams, dated January 30th, 1880. The letter was read, in which Williams warns him not to come there (to Lagrange) to court, for he could give him the names of 20 white men who would kill him for getting up the exodus. They (the colored people) were praying for him, "for you had worked to get them out of this hell, and they would rather be slaves again than live here." The democrats say that "you took the negroes to Indiana to carry the state for the radicals;" that "you (Perry) and John Sherman was the ruin of the south. He had not been there since. Had worked in the Bureau of engraving and printing and in the Second Auditor's office as a laborer. Have a family of seven or eight. Had not left to escape the indictment; and stayed away because he thought he would be murdered. Witness was charged with forgery; did not have anything to do with
Had not left to escape the indictment; and stayed away because he thought he would be murdered. Witness was charged with forgery; did not have anything to do with the forged paper; the other man charged—Aaron E. Perry—was witness' brother. First heard of the accusation in Indianapolis, and when he went back and told the constable, Mr. Morrison, he understood that he had a warrant, and he said he had a paper; this was the latter part of October, 1879. Witness was on the United States grand jury in the spring of 1879. It was generally known that he was there. The next day after he saw the constable he went to the magistrate's office and Mr. Robinson, his lawyer, did not put a witness on the stand. The justice said that something might come out of it, and the three churches raised a coll
samuel-l-perry.A26:
The Alleged Exodus Leader.
HEARING ON HARPAAS CORBES
Yesterday, the hearing of the case of Samuel L. Perry, colored, who has the reputation of having led the negro exodus from North Carolina to Indiana, was continued before Judge Wylie, sitting at chambers in the Columbia Law Building—Messrs. Shellabarger, J. Wilson and R. T. Greener for the petitioner, and Messrs. Merrick and R.S. Davis for the state of North Carolina. Perry, whose extradition to North Carolina to-morrow on a charge of forgery is sought, was subjected to a lengthy cross-examination, in which he said he was born in 1849; that he has had nothing to do with his brother A. E. Perry since 1878, because they supported different candidates. He believed there were people in North Carolina who would murder him. He was a philanthropist while in Indiana supporting the republican party. When he was in the exodus business he ceased to be a politician. He lectured around Legrange in October and November, 1879; went back to make the exodus report, and then went from place to place scattering the exodus ideas. The members of the association were not sworn, but the meetings were secret, and they did not allow any in whom they thought would tell the white people. He and Williams had a contract with Mr. Cole, of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad, to receive $1 per head for each man; but he had not received any of it. Witness took out about 3,000 men, but did not take them out for political purposes; left them at different places. The society furnished the first money and started with only $28, and when they got here they had to walk. Didn't think he could have a fair trial in North Carolina, no matter who defended him, even if colored men were on the jury. The sheriff was a republican and so was the clerk. One white man could lead eleven colored men on a jury.

Re-direct.—The white republicans were opposed to the exodus until after the next election, saying after one more trial if they failed they would advocate the movement. He replied that he did not believe in waiting for salvation, but that they should seek it.

This closed Perry's testimony.

The wife of Perry was called and testified that her husband when he returned after his visit to the west was compelled to hide and dare not sleep at home; men on horseback called at the house and demanded him, but, finding that he was not there, went away; a white lady visited her and told of a plan at work to capture her husband and told her
called at the house and demanded him, but, finding that he was not there, went away; a white lady visited her and told of a plan at work to capture her husband, and told her to advise him to leave there; she was notified by other parties that her husband would be killed if caught.

Mrs. Catherine Perry, the mother of the accused, confirmed the testimony of the preceding witness.

Mr. George K. Bagby, the agent for the state, testified that the indictment was the only reason he knew of for taking Perry back. There was no vindictiveness towards him there on account of the exodus now, whatever there may have been. Adjourned.

INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS TO-DAY—REMARKS OF JUDGE WYLIE.

This morning Mr. Bagbey, the agent of the state, was recalled and subjected to a lengthy cross-examination. Being questioned as to whether this proceeding was not for political purposes, Judge Wylie stopped it, remarking that he was satisfied that this proceeding was taken on account of Perry's connection with the exodus movement and because of his political services to the republican party. Here was a man charged with forgery, for which he had been bailed in $100, the money being collected and paid into the public treasury, and if this man goes back now and is subjected to excessive punishment, what a spectacle before the civilized world. His duty was, however, to decide on the case as presented, and he would not presume that he would be ill treated. If he went back, he would go there with the eyes of the whole country upon him, and the party to which the petitioner belongs having now a majority of officers, he would presume that he would not be without friends.

Mr. Wilson said he proposed to show that the laws were unequally administered, and that the custom was to send colored men to prison for the longest periods for the most trifling crimes.

Mr. Merrick replied that in North Carolina the laws on some subjects were much better than in the District; there are no such offences as brutal assaults on girls of 10 and 12 years of age as there are here; the laws prevent it.

Judge Wylie.—The best law on that subject is Judge Lynch.

Mr. Wilson said he cared not about the law, the custom was what he proposed to show, and it was of frequent occurrence that the highest sentences are imposed and the labor of the negroes farmed out.
the castle was what he proposed to show, and it was of frequent occurrence that the highest sentences are imposed and the labor of the negroes farmed out.

Mr. Merrick.—The farming out of prisoners' labor was borrowed from Massachusetts.

NORTH CAROLINA KU-KLUX.

Mr. Wilson said that they could show that North Carolina was no fit place to send the prisoner, for the highest crimes—such as killing negroes—go unpunished.

Mr. Bagbey testified that he never knew of the ku-klux personally; that there was a case of hanging for rape charged to the ku-klux.

Judge Wylie.—That might have happened in any state.

Mr. Greener asked if Mr. Bagbey had ever heard of ku-klux in the south, and objection being made, the judge remarked that it was a matter of history that there had been such an organization, but the question was, is there such a state of affairs in North Carolina as would prevent the petitioner obtaining a fair trial, and the witness had already testified that he would have a fair trial.

Marshall Douglass was called to testify to the state of society there, but was only able to testify as to being in Raleigh, and knew nothing of Lenoir county.

Mr. Bagbey was recalled and testified that a colored man named Morris, of Lenoir county, had been present up to yesterday, but was not here to-day.

This closed the testimony.

Mr. Wilson made an argument of nearly two hours for the prisoner, and Mr. Davis followed for the state of North Carolina for about an hour. The hearing was at two o'clock adjourned until Monday, when Mr. Merrick will speak and Mr. Greener will close.
samuel-l-perry.A28:
Much Ado About a Black Forger.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 6.—The hearing in the case of Samuel L. Perry, the exodus leader, on a writ of habeas corpus sued out to prevent his removal to North Carolina as a fugitive from justice on charge of raising a school teacher's certificate from $15 to $45, was resumed before Judge Wylie in chambers to-day. G. K. Bagley, agent of the State, was cross-examined by Wilson. Judge Wylie stopped questions which implied a political motive for the remoavl of Perry, saying his duty was to decide on the case as presented and he would not presume that excessive punishment or prosecution would be inflicted on the man if returned. As the eyes of the whole country were on him and as his party was in the majority he would not be without friends. A lively exchange of views took place between Merrick for the State and Wilson, regarding the administration of law in North Carolina, and the existence of the Ku Klux. Prof. Greener asked on behalf of the petitioner if Bagley had ever heard of the Ku Klux, but the question was ruled out. Marshal Fred Douglas was called to testify as to the state of the country, but he had not been in Lenair county. Arguments were then proceeded with and were in progress when the hearing was adjourned until Monday.
samuel-l-perry.A34:
PERRY, THE EYODUS LEADER.
The Writ of Habcas Corpus.
Judge Wylie Releases the Prisoner
This morning Judge Wylie, sitting at Chambers in the Columbia Law Building, rendered his decision in the case of Samuel L. Perry, the alleged exodus leader, who was arrested here on a requisition from North Carolina, charging him with forgery in that state. Perry, after being placed in the hands of the agent of the state by order of Judge Cartter, was subsequently brought before him (Judge Wylie) on writ of habeas corpus. The arguments before Judge Wylie were concluded on Monday—Messrs. Shellabarger, Wilson and R. T. Greener for the petitioner and Messrs. R. T. Merrick and R. S. Davis for the state. Judge Wylie took his seat on the bench at 10% o'clock this morning, and remarked that he had in the brief interval since the argument given the case as much consideration as he was able to, recounted the circumstances of the arrest on the warrant of the chief justice, the delivery of Perry to Mr. Bagbey, the agent of the state, who presented the requisition, etc. He read the papers, remarking on the address, "His excellency," that we have no such titles here and they should not be used. A copy of the indictment is also appended as required, and these papers were presented to the chief justice as the executive, the legislative powers having placed this duty on him. Strictly and utterly the District is not within the terms of the constitution as to the extradition of prisoners, but we are bound by the law. The chief justice had decided that Perry was a fugitive from justice, and made a warrant for his return, and the writ of habeas corpus was applied for setting forth improper restraint of liberty, juncece of the crime charged, and restraining the objections made before the chief justice. It is not worth while at this day to examine authorities to learn whether the writ of habeas corpus would lie in such a case, for that was settled. He must proceed to inquire into the cause of detention, &c. The petitioner sets forth that the requisition was not issued for public good—not in the interest of public justice—but it was in the spirit of envy and mahce, because he had encouraged the exodus, and that this proceeding was fabricated to bring him to punishment for his activity in that cause; and he further says that if sent back he would not have a fair trial, and his life would be in danger. Under the law these allegations could be inquired into. He doubted whether he had made out a case on those points, although he had offered some witnesses and presented some letters on that point. This is all contradicted by Mr. Bagbey, and he says that Perry's life will be perfectly safe, that he will have a fair trial, &c. The court was inclined to believe that he (Perry) would be perfectly safe, especially as he had friends who would see justice done. He could not believe that such a state of affairs as was represented exists in North Carolina to-day. The presumption of the constitution is that fair trials will be given. Local prejudices may spring up and prevent a fair, impartial trial, but constitutional laws are not to be administered under any idea that fair and impartial trials will not follow. He thought if the relator had not made out a case he should be returned to North Carolina and submit himself to the law. It had been claimed that the office of the Chief Justice in such cases is ministerial only, but he (the court) could not believe it. He read the statute on the subject (sec. 5,278), and said that a requisition without an indictment or affidavit would be a nullity. The executive is to look at the indictment and affidavit, and find if the charge has been made out and also if he is a fugitive. This latter fact must be shown also. In this case it appears Perry was arrested on this charge a year after the charge was made and held to bail, and his friends raised the money. It must therefore be presumed that he was aware of the charge, and it is shown that he left there a few days afterwards. The evidence shows, at least, a prima facie case of fleeing from justice. He is, technically, a fugitive from justice. The alleged forged paper bears date of December 20, 1875, and nothing was done until the fall of 1879 (October). Perry having in the meantime be come engaged in the exodus movement, leaving Lenoir county September 15th. The feeling against him was hostile and he was warned not to return, but he went back and, like a prudent man, kept his friends about him. He was, now ever, arrested and gave bail, and in April, 1880, the indictment was found. It seemed that this man prepared the paper but did not utter it, and when arrested putting up a hundred dollars which the state has, he left the state, and it is strange that a public officer should hunt the man down. What kind of bail is $100 for forgery? He (the court) was strongly impressed that there was nothing in the case. Though technically a fugitive from justice Perry was not intentionally for he thought that the $100 having been put up for him the case was ended. Reading the indictment and endorsements showing by witnesses on the back, two of whom testified before the grand jury, the court said that the whole moral atmosphere around the case is suspicious. Mr. Bagbey, the agent of the state, is a farmer of Lenoir county, from the very scene of the heat of excitement, which is another suspicious circumstance. Usually sheriffs or some such officers are made the agents in such cases, but here is a private citizen. The forged paper reads, "The treasurer will pay," and it is not an order that he shall pay, nor is it addressed to the treasurer. He then pointed out a defect in the indictment—no averment being set out that the parties purporting to have drawn the order were the school committee, as was decided necessary in the case of North Carolina against Bob Thorn, in the supreme court in that state. There was no averment that bad the paper been genuine, it would have been good. He regarded the paper as no order at all, and the indictment to be defective. He would therefore discharge this man from arrest. He believed that the man was of fair character, and he did not believe it would be for the public good to send him back. Then there was no certainty of his having a speedy trial, and he was gratified that under the law he could conscientiously discharge this man. He was certain North Carolina would not suffer by the man not going back, for under a fair trial he could not be convicted. Under these proceedings it belonged to the judge to examine as to the crime, and if satisfied that there was none, to discharge the party. Under the comity between nations, no nation would surrender a man under such papers as these. This man being a citizen of the republic, would be permitted to remain here or go where he pleases. Having lived here a year with the presumptions in his favor, he will remain. It was announced that Mr. Merrick would take an appeal.

During the delivery of this decision the crowd (nine-tenths of it being colored men) gradually increased until there were about 75 in the room, and it included a number of colored ministers, Cadet Whittaker, and the wife of Perry.
samuel-l-perry.A40:
The Case of "Exoduster" Perry.
In the Supreme Court in general term this morning, the appeal case of Samuel L. Perry, the negro who, as our readers may recollect, was the principal agent in inducing the negroes of North Carolina to emigrate to Indiana prior to the late Presidential election, was called up for a hearing. The facts are these: The Governor of North Carolina made a requisition upon the proper authorities of the District for the rendition of Samuel L. Perry, a negro man, indicted in North Carolina for the crime of forgery. The accused was surrendered upon the requisition, but before his removal by the agent of the State, a habeas corpus was served out before Judge Wylie, who discharged him. Thereupon Mr. R. T. Merrick, counsel for the State of North Carolina, brought the case to the general term on appeal from Judge Wylie's decision. Mr. R. T. Merrick for the State and Mr. R. S. Davis contra; argument in progress.

wright-sumter-county-1880-12-30.A1: KILLED BY AN OFFICER.—In Sumter county, S. C., yesterday, a colored thief named Wright in resisting arrest cut and shot Deputy Sheriff Bateman. Wright was then shot and killed by another deputy. Bateman's wounds are serious.
wright-sumter-county-1880-12-30.A2:
Killed While Resisting Arrest.
CHAMLESTON S. C. December 30 - A sp
CHARLESTON, S. C., December 30.—A special to the News and Courier reports that in Sumter county to-day a colored man named Wright, for whom a warrant had been issued for stealing a bale of cotton, resisted, and cut and shot a deputy sheriff named Bateman, who attempted to arrest him, and was then shot and killed by another deputy sheriff. Bateman's wounds are serious.
wright-sumter-county-1880-12-30.A5:
Three Murders Yesterday.
A colored man, name 1 Wright seriously wounded a deputy sheriff named Bateman, who was, trying to arrest him and was then shot dead by another deputy, in Sumpter county, South Carolina, yesterday. John Williams was stabbed to death by George Tucker in a drunken quarrel, in Halifax county, Virginia, a few days ago. A warrant has been issued in St Louis for the arrest of Mary Grover, who is charged with having placed her baby on a vacant lot and allowed it to freeze to death, last Sunday night.
wright-sumter-county-1880-12-30.A7:
There was terrible loss of life at the burning of a New York tenement house. Tuesday, Eleven women and children were burnt.

Mr. St. Vincent, in Central Park, was burned Sunday, loss over $100,000.

The New York Senatorial canvass has begun; Mr. Depew is promised strong support in the Senate, and Mr. Platt and Mr. Crowley are actively at work.

It is reported that prominent Republicans have been invited to visit President-elect Garfield at Mentor and advise as to his cabinet.

One of Sitting Bull's chiefs has surrendered a number of lodges and preparations are making to receive the surrender of the rest of his band.

The Rev. Myron Adams, of Rochester, N.Y., has been cut off from fellowship with the Congregational Church.

Franz Lammens and Mrs. Meirhoeffer are to be hanged at Newark, this week.

A bank clerk at Fall River, Mass., has proved a defaulter.

The estimates of the New York Police Board have been cut down over $400,000.

District-Attorney Benjamin K. Phelps died Wednesday night.

In Sumter County, S. C., on the 20th, ult., a deputy sheriff killed a negro.

Intensely cold weather was reported from different parts of the country, last week; several persons were frozen to death.

Friday was the coldest day in New York city since 1875; the lowest record of the thermometer was 5° below zero.

The capitol at Albany is considered safe, despite the recently discovered defect.

The Republicans have elected the Speaker of the Tennessee House of Representatives.

On Monday Henry Burton, of Memphis, shot his wife and a man named Tate, and then Tate killed Burton.

The Republicans have organized both Houses of the California Legislature.

The defeat of Mr. Grow for the Senate in Pennsylvania seems settled upon.

The Puleman Palace Car Co. has been defeated in a Baltimore case.
wright-sumter-county-1880-12-30.A9:
ITEMS FROM ROCKINHAM SPIRIT. — Mr. E. W. Marship, of Wolf Pit Township, has removed, with his family, to our city, and will soon open a bar-room in the "Rockets" near that of Mr. E. A. McDonald. — Rev. N. T. Bowden will shortly take a school 18 miles above here. — Capt. James T. Bradley, one of our excellent board of County Commissioners, will remove to Wadesboro where he will engage in the mercantile business. — The "South Union Mills," on Hitchcock Creek, belonging to the estate of the late Gen. Alfred Dockery were sold at public auction on the 4th inst; Mr. T. Benson Ledbetter becoming the purchaser, $2,500; Mr. Ledbetter will at once perfect arrangements for the erection of a cotton factory on the site. — We spoke, last week, of Mr. E. H. Bateman, deputy sheriff of Sumter county, S. C., and brother of Mr. A. J. Bateman, of this town, having been shot by a negro. It seems he was struck on the head by the negro with a cooking vessel, knocking him down and breaking the "spider" in pieces. His wounds, though severe, are not serious. The negro who was shot through the head and instantly killed, by Mr. Peter Mallett, was charged with stealing a bale of cotton from Mr. James H. Aycock, formerly of this town. If we are not mistaken, Mr. Mallett is a native of Fayetteville, this State. The Coroner's jury returned a verdict of "justifiable homicide." The negro had a pistol and was endeavoring to use it and Mallet did not fire until requested to do so by Bateman. — The body of James Haddock, the young man referred to last week as missing, was found in the Pee Dee Factory pound last Sunday. His gun was found some distance from his body and in water not over four or five feet deep. He probably broke through the ice here, and in endeavoring to reach the nearest point of land to him, got into deep water. He had stripped himself of both his overcoat and dress coat. Coroner Gay held an inquest. The corpse is said by those saw it to have presented a most strange appearance. The cheeks were red and rosy—the eyes and mouth closed, there being nothing to indicate but that he was merely sleeping—being in robust health.

He was an Irishman about 27 years of age, and, we understand, was engaged to be married soon.
